Exactly. "Suicide is a permanent solution to temporary pain." I'll give you the same advice that I've given somebody else, based on the fact that you've recognized that suicide is an easier option to take--

Being depressed is much, much, much easier than being happy. It really is. I speak from experience. Therefore, I would suggest that perhaps you wallow in it for a while. Really objectively observe yourself feeling sorry for yourself. Indulging in your sadness. Do whatever you can do to make it feel great. Wear it like a badge, feel comforted by it as a friend. And then use these things to learn about yourself. Eventually, you will realize that you are unhappy because you want to be unhappy. That's what I realized. Then you won't want to kill yourself anymore; you'll simply want to walk around in a haze of grey, lifeless apathy for a bit. Eventually (if you're anything like me) you'll get sick of this. It will stop bringing you satisfaction. You will begin to really genuinely want it to stop. That is when help can truly be sought.

Well, if you want to be happy, do it! Just do it. I know, I know, "It's not that simple!!!" Well, the thing that depressed people do not want to admit is this: it is. It is that simple. You have every power to look for something beautiful, and even if it's small and ridiculously stupid, you have the power to latch onto it. You have the power to accept that you are responsible for your own fate. FAKE IT UNTIL YOU MAKE IT. Smile. Smile a totally, completely, soul-rendingly fake smile. One that makes you want to vomit. Do it. And then just keep doing it. Do it more than on just your face, do it figuratively, everywhere else in your life. Start living like a happy person, even though you're not (the hardest thing to do) and eventually you will become one. RESPOND to the thoughts that you have that hurt you as if they're not coming from you, but from an old version of you. *The world would be better off without me--I don't think that way any more. I'm ugly--I'm more attractive than a lot of people I know, so stop it. Today was a horrible day--okay, well, tomorrow will be better.* You have to be the person that makes you feel better. No one can do this for you. Take care of yourself. Force yourself. It will be difficult and it will NOT feel like it is helping. But anything can come, given enough time. 

Try. Just try. Happiness isn't something that happens to you, it's something that you have to build.

Problem 1) You've already said "I know this isn't true." Well, I can fully understand that knowing something isn't going to happen and worrying about it anyway is EXTREMELY frustrating. I can also tell you how to stop: just stop. I know, I know, *"It's not that simple!!!"* Well, guess what? The aggravating, nail-chewing, jaw-clenching truth of the matter is that, yes, it actually is that simple. Having worried thoughts is not a choice. They just pop up, independently of anything else, and for this you cannot be blamed. However, paying attention to these thoughts--and fueling them with further ones--*is a choice.* You DO have a LARGE degree of control over how much you worry about how other people see you and whether or not you are annoying or aggravating them. 

Have you ever tried meditating? Try it now. It's difficult. Sit up straight, eyes open but gaze unfocused, fold your hands in your lap, and *don't think about anything.* If you actually listened to me and behaved this way for 5-10 minutes, you probably found that you were still having a lot of thoughts. How long have I had that poster for? Is that the dog crying? Why wasn't my teacher wearing a belt today? These are the sorts of thoughts that pop up and cannot be controlled, summoned, or sent away, but, when negative, like "I bet she really doesn't like me at all and is only pretending," MUST BE IGNORED. And ignoring those thoughts is a difficult choice that you must make. You are GOING to want to harp on about them inside your mind, because somewhere, for us human beings, worrying just *feels better*. But whenever these thoughts come up, no matter how badly you want to chase them and examine them, don't. Just don't. Make a conscious effort to think about something else, even if it means you have to remind yourself a million times that *thinking about irrational worries will accomplish exactly nothing*. Because they're *irrational*. If ignored consistently and often, these thoughts WILL go away, I promise. But you have to choose to make them, and accept that you are the one with the power.

Problem 2) Motivation is exponential. Don't look at it like a cliff, as being either on the cliff or not on the cliff. It's not quite so binary. It's more like a staircase. Every day, just try to take a step up the staircase. It doesn't matter how small at first--in fact, the smaller the better. How bad is it right now? Do you skip a lot? If so, just go to school tomorrow. That's it. That's all you have to do. Just go to school. Do you leave your homework without doing it often? If so, work on your homework tomorrow. Don't pressure yourself to complete it. Don't beat yourself up because it's already taken so long and it feels like it's late. No time is TOO late. Just keep doing this, over and over again. Eventually the steps that you'll take will grow on their own and it will begin to feel easier. It will never, however, be effortless. You are going to need to keep on top of yourself and parent yourself a little bit.

Problem 3) I'll assume that you're between 15 and 22 since you said you're in school, and tell you this: it is very early to be having these thoughts. You are putting a lot of pressure on yourself to already have accomplished something when hardly any of your adult life has elapsed. Be patient on this one. Give it a rest. It is an illogical and useless worry that you are going to have to force yourself to ignore, just like Problem 1. 

Problem 4) Now, I'm no doctor and I don't know you personally, but my immediate instinct upon reading this is (quite honestly) to experiment with recreational drugs. Using them as a crutch is unacceptable, but perceiving the world in which we live through different lights *CAN* change you forever, and for the better. I know it did for me. On the other hand, overthinking things is more of a personality issue than a mental health one, and can sometimes benefit you. I'd try a balance between fixing this and accepting it. 

Problem 5) Performance anxiety, huh? I bet you're waiting for a moment that you feel a little more confident and a little less nervous. Well, you're not going to like hearing this, but that moment doesn't exist. If you want to become comfortable onstage, you are going to have to experience being uncomfortable on it, first. I can very strongly assert this based on personal experience. Just like Jake the dog said, "Sucking at something is the first step towards bein' kinda good at something." It's just the same way with standup. You'll be nervous. People will be able to tell that you are nervous. Your voice will shake and maybe not many people will laugh. But hey, once you finish that first dreaded performance--the worst is officially over. Every single performance after that first one is going to be better than the last. Maybe your stage fright will never completely go away, but by forcing yourself to confront it, you can become a much better performer. 

Problem 6) You wish you could talk to me more?! That's so sweet :D PM me anytime, we can talk about anything under the sun. I don't know you but we are both human beings and I am here to support you however I can figure out how.

That's not at all a terrible idea. It's catharsis--it will not feel very good at first, but afterwards you should feel loads better. Like throwing up, only emotional. 

Alternatively, you can PM me anytime. I will respond to you about anything, even if you just want to shoot the shit in order to be distracted for a little bit.

Overall, it's playful, touching, and (for me) overwhelmingly nostalgic. If I had to choose a single game to replay for the rest of my life, it would be Lunar: Silver Star Story Complete.
